library(tidyverse)
# Add any other libraries here
library(readr)
library(janitor)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(lubridate)
library(rsample)
Raw Variable Name Clean Variable Name Data Type Numerical or Categorical Description & Units
Date date chr categorical date in year-month-day format
Rented Bike Count rented_bike_count dbl numerical count of bikes rented at each hour
Hour hour dbl numerical hour of the day
Temperature temperature_c dbl numerical temperature in Celsius
Humidity humidity_percent dbl numerical humidity in percentage
Wind Speed wind_speed_m_s dbl numerical wind speed in m/s
Visibility visibility_10m dbl numerical visibility in 10m units
Dew Point Temperature dew_point_temperature_c dbl numerical dew point temperature - temperature at which the air needs to be cooled to (at constant pressure) in order to achieve a relative humidity
Solar Radiation solar_radiation_mj_m2 dbl numerical solar radiation in MJ/M^2
Rainfall rainfall_mm dbl numerical rainfall in mm
Snowfall snowfall_cm dbl numerical snowfall in cm
Seasons seasons chr categorical represents the four seasons
Holiday holiday chr categorical holiday or no holiday
Functioning Day functioning_day chr categorical yes or no; represents if system is fully operational or not

Questions

  1. Does temperature affect bike demand differently during peak commuting hours (8-9am and 6-7pm) compared to off-peak hours?
  2. Is the holiday effect uniform across seasons, or do holiday demand patterns shift significantly between the seasons?
  3. Is there a sharp threshold or non-linear drop-off point where precipitation severly degrades demand, or is the decay linear?
  4. How do temperature and humidity combine to affect demand (compared to just considering temperature)?
  5. How does the hourly distribution shift between a regular working day and a non-working day?

Task 1 - Investigating the Effect of Temperature of Number of Rented Bikes During Peak or Non-Peak Hours

1.1 Data Wrangling

We define peak commuting hours as 7-9am and 5-7pm

#Task 1
seoul_bikes <- seoul_bikes |> 
  mutate(
    peak = ifelse(hour %in% c(7:9, 17:19), TRUE, FALSE)
    #used Gemini to help with shortening the conditional statement, as initially was hour == 7 | hour == 8 | ... 
  )

1.2a Data Visualisation (Scatterplot)

#Task 1 - evaluating temperature sensitivty during peak hours vs. off-peak hours
seoul_bikes |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = temperature_c, y = rented_bike_count)) +
  geom_jitter(
    aes(colour = peak),
    alpha = 0.15
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "gam",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.2,
    colour = "#d95f02"
    ) +
  facet_grid( #changed to facet_grid to take holidays into account, not taking weekdays vs. weekends into account as there many weekend workers in Seoul who may need to commute
    holiday ~ peak,
    labeller = as_labeller(c("TRUE" = "Peak", "FALSE" = "Non-Peak", "Holiday" = "Holiday", "No Holiday" = "Working Day"))
    ) +
  #changes labels from facetting to "Peak" and "Non-Peak"
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_colour_manual(
    guide = "legend",
    values = c("TRUE" = "#384860", "FALSE" = "#97a6c4"), #changed colour to lighter shades, as otherwise points are too dark
    labels = c("TRUE" = "Peak", "FALSE" = "Non-Peak")
    ) +
  guides(alpha = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Temperature (c)",
    y = "Number of Rented Bikes Per Hour",
    colour = "Peak Commuting Hour (7-9am or 5-7pm)",
    title = "Bike Demand Sensitivity to Temperature"
  )
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ s(x, bs = "cs")'

From the difference in the opacities/ darkness of each scatterplot, we can see that the dataset contains many more entries for non-peak hours than peak hours.

We can also see this from the following code:

seoul_bikes |> 
  group_by(peak) |> 
  count()
## # A tibble: 2 × 2
## # Groups:   peak [2]
##   peak      n
##   <lgl> <int>
## 1 FALSE  6347
## 2 TRUE   2118

However, we can already see there might be similarities in the pattern or the shape of the data represented above, where unimodal, asymmetric clusters can be seen for the two groups.

From the points during peak commuting hours, we see its maximum is much higher than that of the non-peak hours, the values specifically are 3556 vs. 2579 bikes/ hour.

On average, we also see that the number of rented bikes per hour is significantly higher during peak hours, with the means being approx. 1052 vs. 621, and the medians being 867 vs. 440.

The spread of data between peak and non-peak hours are also quite different, where the standard deviation for peak and non-peak hours are approx. 798 vs. 540 bikes/ hour and the interquartile range being approx 1290 vs. 772. This may suggest that the number of bikes that are rented during off peak times might be less predictable or less stable. However, it must also be noted that we have not removed holidays from this plot, so the peak hours may also include weekends and holidays, where no work is conducted. The spread of data exclusively on working days may be less spread out for peak times in particular.

Additionally, if we consider the GAM line on the scatterplot, we see that the line for the peak hours are much steeper than that of the non-peak hours, which may suggest that temperature acts as a stronger multiplier during peak hours.

We also see that the resiliance of commuters during lower temperatures (colder weather) at peak times is stronger, this would imply that commuters are less likely to not commute with bikes, as they must get to work or get to school on time. Conversely, for those during off-peak hours, the lower coldness tolerance may suggest they are less reliant on renting bikes and may choose to stay indoors or opt for another form of transport entirely.

Back to the similarities, we see that at high heat, the number of rented bikes per hour drop off. This means that once a threshold of around 30 degrees C is hit, even the peak commuters will choose another way of commuting, likely travelling with transportation offerring air-conditioning, e.g. busses or the metro.

To be more specific, we shall analyse the distribution of the data, we should instead consider the density plots:

determine_density_maxes <- function(df, max_var, max_var_condition, density_var){ #parameters to keep generality of function
  density_df <- df |>
    filter({{ max_var }} == max_var_condition) |>
    pull({{ density_var }}) |> 
    density() |> 
    (\(d) tibble::tibble(x = d$x, y = d$y))()
    #creating a separate data frame for density values
  
    high_peak <- density_df |> filter(y == max(y))
    low_peak <- density_df |> filter(x < 15) |> filter(y == max(y))
    
    tibble::tibble(
      max_y_high = high_peak$y,
      x_at_max_y_high = high_peak$x,
      max_y_low = low_peak$y,
      x_at_max_y_low = low_peak$x
    )
    #returns values in tibble form
    
}
#needed to use {{}} as passing in the column names and not variable objects - Gemini was used, as it was initially causing errors

peak_maxes<- determine_density_maxes(seoul_bikes, peak, TRUE, temperature_c)
non_peak_maxes <- determine_density_maxes(seoul_bikes, peak, FALSE, temperature_c)

peak_maxes
## # A tibble: 1 × 4
##   max_y_high x_at_max_y_high max_y_low x_at_max_y_low
##        <dbl>           <dbl>     <dbl>          <dbl>
## 1     0.0297            22.1    0.0250           3.56
non_peak_maxes
## # A tibble: 1 × 4
##   max_y_high x_at_max_y_high max_y_low x_at_max_y_low
##        <dbl>           <dbl>     <dbl>          <dbl>
## 1     0.0317            21.1    0.0255           4.94
#followed the following guide: https://ianmadd.github.io/pages/PeakDensityDistribution.html

seoul_bikes |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = temperature_c, alpha = 0.1, colour = ifelse(peak == TRUE, "#384860", "#97a6c4"))) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = peak_maxes$x_at_max_y_high, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#384860") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = peak_maxes$x_at_max_y_low, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#384860") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = non_peak_maxes$x_at_max_y_high, linetype = "dotted", colour = "#97a6c4") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = non_peak_maxes$x_at_max_y_low, linetype = "dotted", colour = "#97a6c4") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_colour_identity(
    guide = "legend",
    labels = c("Peak", "Non-Peak")
    ) +
  guides(alpha = "none") +
  labs(
    x = "Temperature (c)",
    y = "Density",
    colour = "Peak Commuting Hour (7-9am or 6-7pm)",
    title = stringr::str_wrap("Temperature Distribution Comparison : Peak and Non-Peak Commuting Hours")
    #needed str_wrap to ensure the entire title shows on the plot
  )

Just looking at the shape of the curves, they are both clearly bimodal (i.e. two distinct peaks) and at specific points. Each peak in each of the density plots are highlighted by the vertical dashed or dotted line passing through them, with the corresponding colours matching if it is for the peak times or non-peak times plots.

We can see that both plots resemble the same shape, essentially an “M”, where the right peak is slightly higher than the one on the left.

This may indicate how the relative proportions of how bike-renters reacting to changes in temperatures are almost identical across peak and off-peak commuting hours.

#Task 2 Determining if the drop in demand for rented bikes is consistent across all four seasons(Specifically when it is a holiday).

Is the effect of holidays on bike rental demand is consistent across all four seasons?

Does adverse weather have a consistent impact on bike rental demand during holidays across all four seasons?

I’ll need to group data - season - holiday - hour compare vs non-holiday in each season visualise results work out percentages/mean differences in data that allows a conclusion # 2.1 Grouping data by rented bike count holiday vs no holiday

holiday_comparison <- seoul_bikes %>%
  group_by(holiday) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_rentals = mean(rented_bike_count, na.rm = TRUE),
   )

#2.2 Bar chart of rented bike count holiday vs no holiday

ggplot(holiday_comparison,
       aes(x = holiday, y = avg_rentals, fill = holiday)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Average bike rentals during a holiday vs non-holiday",
    x = "Holiday vs Non-Holiday",
    y = "Average number of bikes rented"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Observations: Very simple bar chart and code shows that on average there is more bike rentals during non-holiday days vs holiday days. Is this suprising? For me it was slightly suprising (presuming this is seouls holiday) you might have thought people get out and about explore the city more, if tourists come over you definetly might presume they rent out bikes. On the contrary many workers may leave the city for the holiday and therefore bike rental decreases. The no holiday rental was 739 compared to holiday rental average of 529. 39.7% difference ((739-529)/529)x100. Regular commuting patterns may also explain this. We can’t determine the cause though with this one data viz.

#2.3 Grouping data with seasons now included

season_holiday_comparison <- seoul_bikes %>%
  group_by(seasons, holiday) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_rentals = mean(rented_bike_count, na.rm = TRUE),

Observations: This grouped bar chart shows how the average bike rentals varies between holidays and non-holidays across the four seasons. ##Task 3

Identify if precipitation drops demand linearly or shows a sharp threshold

We look at rental counts at various levels of precipitation to see if demand decreases gradually as precipitation increases or drops off sharply above a certain point.

library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)

# 3.1. Load the full Seoul Bike CSV.
bikes <- read_csv(
  "data/SeoulBikeData.csv",
  locale = locale(encoding = "latin1")
) %>%
  clean_names()
## Rows: 8760 Columns: 14
## ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## Delimiter: ","
## chr  (4): Date, Seasons, Holiday, Functioning Day
## dbl (10): Rented Bike Count, Hour, Temperature(°C), Humidity(%), Wind speed ...
## 
## ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
## ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
# 3.2 Keep only hours when the bike rental service was operating.
bikes <- bikes %>%
  filter(functioning_day == "Yes")
# 3.3 Each row represents one hour. | means OR, and & means AND.
wet_hours <- bikes %>%
  filter(rainfall_mm > 0 | snowfall_cm > 0)

both_hours <- bikes %>%
  filter(rainfall_mm > 0 & snowfall_cm > 0)

wet_hours %>%
  summarise(hours = n())
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##   hours
##   <int>
## 1   931
both_hours %>%
  summarise(hours = n())
## # A tibble: 1 × 1
##   hours
##   <int>
## 1    28

931 hours had snow,rain or both 28hours had both rain and snow

# 3.4 Compare rain and snow separately, keeping dry hours in both plots.
rain_data <- bikes %>%
  filter(snowfall_cm == 0)

snow_data <- bikes %>%
  filter(rainfall_mm == 0)
# Define precipitation bands
rain_data <- rain_data %>%
  mutate(
    rain_level = case_when(
      rainfall_mm == 0 ~ "0",
      rainfall_mm > 0 & rainfall_mm <= 1 ~ "(0, 1]",
      rainfall_mm > 1 & rainfall_mm <= 5 ~ "(1, 5]",
      rainfall_mm > 5 & rainfall_mm <= 10 ~ "(5, 10]",
      rainfall_mm > 10 ~ ">10"
    ),
    rain_level = fct_relevel(
      rain_level,
      "0", "(0, 1]", "(1, 5]", "(5, 10]", ">10"
    )
  )

snow_data <- snow_data %>%
  mutate(
    snow_level = case_when(
      snowfall_cm == 0 ~ "0",
      snowfall_cm > 0 & snowfall_cm <= 1 ~ "(0, 1]",
      snowfall_cm > 1 & snowfall_cm <= 3 ~ "(1, 3]",
      snowfall_cm > 3 & snowfall_cm <= 5 ~ "(3, 5]",
      snowfall_cm > 5 ~ ">5"
    ),
    snow_level = fct_relevel(
      snow_level,
      "0", "(0, 1]", "(1, 3]", "(3, 5]", ">5"
    )
  )
# Rainfall box plot: exclude snow to isolate rainfall
ggplot(
  data = rain_data,
  mapping = aes(x = rain_level, y = rented_bike_count)
) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Bike rentals by rainfall level",
    x = "Rainfall (mm)",
    y = "Hourly bike rentals"
  )

# Snowfall box plot: exclude rain to isolate snowfall
ggplot(
  data = snow_data,
  mapping = aes(x = snow_level, y = rented_bike_count)
) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightgrey") +
  labs(
    title = "Bike rentals by snowfall level",
    x = "Snowfall (cm)",
    y = "Hourly bike rentals"
  )

Both box plots show significantly lower median bike rentals during hours with precipitation. The largest drop is between zero precipitation and the lowest positive precipitation band, suggesting a possible threshold for the initiation of rain or snow. Demand for rainfall falls further at higher levels, while snowfall has a less consistent pattern. These results suggest a nonlinear relationship but the group plots cannot identify a specific threshold. Differences may also be due to other factors like temperature, season and time of day.

# 3.6 Check the number of hours and the median rentals in each band.
rain_summary <- rain_data %>%
  group_by(rain_level) %>%
  summarise(
    hours = n(),
    median_rentals = median(rented_bike_count, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

snow_summary <- snow_data %>%
  group_by(snow_level) %>%
  summarise(
    hours = n(),
    median_rentals = median(rented_bike_count, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

rain_summary
## # A tibble: 5 × 3
##   rain_level hours median_rentals
##   <fct>      <int>          <dbl>
## 1 0           7534            643
## 2 (0, 1]       256            127
## 3 (1, 5]       169             38
## 4 (5, 10]       42             22
## 5 >10           21             51
snow_summary
## # A tibble: 5 × 3
##   snow_level hours median_rentals
##   <fct>      <int>          <dbl>
## 1 0           7534            643
## 2 (0, 1]       240            144
## 3 (1, 3]       128            178
## 4 (3, 5]        44             86
## 5 >5             3            114

Median hourly bike rentals dropped from 643 at dry hours to 127 with rainfall above 0 and up to 1mm, which is a decrease of about 80%. The median then fell to 38 for raifall between 1 and 5mm and 22 between 5 and 10mm. It increased when above 10mm to 51, this band contained only 21 observations. The greatest decrease happened between dry conditions and light rain, meaning a possible threshold near the start of rain.

Snowfall showed a similar initial drop. Median rentals decreased from 643 with no precipitation to 144 with snowfall above 0 and up to 1 cm, a decrease of approximately 78%. The medians across higher snowfall bands were 178, 86 and 114, showing an inconsistent pattern. The highest snowfall band contained only three observations, making its median unclear.

To sum things up these results at first show a big reduction in percipitation rather than a slow and steady decline.We cannot establish a threshold using the data ## Task 4

seoul_bikes |> ggplot(aes(x = temperature_c, y = humidity_percent,
                          z = rented_bike_count
                      )) + stat_summary_2d(
                        fun = mean, aes(fill
                                        = after_stat(value))
                      ) + scale_fill_viridis_c() + 
                          labs(x = "Temperature (Degrees Celsius)",
                               y = "Humidity (%)",
                               fill = "Rented Bike Count",
                               title = "Bikes Rented according to Temperature and Humidity")

Looking at the graph, we can see that bikes are rented most when temperature is between 20 and 25 degrees and humidity is relatively low. The sales drop off to often below 500 bikes rented per hour on average whenever temperature is below zero regardless of humidity, and there is a similar drop off when humidity nears 100% although to a less extreme extent. This implies that temperature is a greater concern when people are deciding whether or not to rent bikes, which makes intuitive sense as it is a more immediately noticeable factor.

#used genAI to help with creating variables to run code

seoul_bikes <- seoul_bikes %>%
  mutate(
    day_type = if_else(
      lubridate::wday(as.Date(date, format = "%d/%m/%Y"),
                      week_start = 1) >= 6 | holiday == "Holiday",
      "Weekend/Holiday",
      "Weekday"
    )
  )
hour_profile <- seoul_bikes |>
group_by(day_type, hour) |>
summarise( 
mean_rented_bikes = mean(`rented_bike_count`,na.rm = TRUE),
.groups = "drop"
)

ggplot(hour_profile, aes(x = hour, y = mean_rented_bikes, colour = day_type)) +
geom_line() +
labs(x = "Hour", y = "Mean rented bikes", colour = "Day type"
) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, by = 2)) +
theme_minimal()

hour_profile |>
group_by(day_type) |>
slice_max(mean_rented_bikes, n = 1)
## # A tibble: 2 × 3
## # Groups:   day_type [2]
##   day_type         hour mean_rented_bikes
##   <chr>           <dbl>             <dbl>
## 1 Weekday            18             1766.
## 2 Weekend/Holiday    17             1141.

The graph shows that weekday and weekend bike rentals follow different pattern throughout the day. Wekkday rentals have a sharp morning peak at 8 am, followed by a decrease before rising again to its highest point at 6pm, with an average of 1724 rentals. Weekend/holiday rentals increase more gradually throughout the day, reaching the highest point at 5pm, with an average of 1161 rentals. Overall, weekday rentals are generally higher during peak commuting hours, while weekend/holiday rentals are more evenly spread throughout the day. This suggests that weekday bike usage is most influenced by commuting patterns. Another noticeable difference is that weekday rentals rise much more sharply between 6am and 8am, suggesting increased demand during the morning commute. In contrast, weekend/ holiday rentals reach higher levels later in the morning and afternoon but without the sudden increase. During the early hours of the morning, both day types experince relatively low rental numbers, with the lowest levels occurring around 4-5 am. Towards the end of the day, rentals decrease for both groups, particularly after 10pm. These differences suggest that the time of day has an important influence on bike rental demand, and that the reasons for using bikes differs between weekdays and weekends/holidays.

  #although can consider peak and non-peak hours, the afternoon hours overall suggest that demand still remains high, so it would be wrong to group the afternoon hours with other times. As such, it might be worth dropping the peak variable.

Variables to Drop

  1. dew_point_temperature_c has high correlation to temperature_c and humidity_percent, this functions essentially as a compounded variable for rented_bike_count, so we can drop this.

  2. visibility, whilst it has a moderately strong negative correlation with humidity_percent, as it ultimately still has a weak correlation with rented_bike_count, we can drop this too.

  3. wind_speed_m_s is by far the least corrolative variable with rented_bike_count, we can drop this as well.

  4. peak seems to be outperformed by the hour variable, which is unsurprising, as it servers more as a generalisation. As such it might be worth dropping it, as the reason for such a low correlation is because afternoon demand still remains high, although it is always lower than the peak hours. Thus, we will drop this variable as well.

  5. solar radiation, although it has some correlation to the number of rented bikes, it does not have a significant correlation with other variables except temperature, wind speed and humidity. As we will keep temperature and hunidity, and are dropping wind speed, this will also be dropped for simplicity.

To simplify the model, we might want to group variables together into new ones, such as for rainfall_mm and snowfall_cm, we may be able to mutate these into a new variable called precipitation. Perhaps we can model this as just a binary variable, as in many days within the data there was neither.

#We merge rainfall and snowfall variables together, and consider weekdays & weekends, and also join hour and holiday together as their behaviours are different based on whether it is a holiday or not.
seoul_bikes <- seoul_bikes |> 
  mutate(
    precipitation = ifelse(rainfall_mm > 0 | snowfall_cm > 0, 1, 0),
    is_weekend   = wday(dmy(date)) %in% c(1, 7),
    hour_holiday = interaction(hour, holiday, sep = "_")
  ) |> 
  select(
    rented_bike_count,
    hour_holiday,
    is_weekend,
    temperature_c,
    humidity_percent,
    seasons,
    precipitation
  )

seoul_bikes <- seoul_bikes %>%
  mutate(
    wind_group = cut(
      wind_speed_m_s,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 1, 2, 3, 4, Inf),
      labels = c("0-1", "1-2", "2-3", "3-4", "4+")
    )
  )

ggplot(seoul_bikes,
       aes(x = wind_group,
           y = rented_bike_count)) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "col",
    fill = "steelblue"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Bike Rentals at Different Wind Speeds",
